question: How can Chinese natural language understanding be evaluated in a standard, GLUE-style way, given that existing NLU benchmarks are almost all English?
hypothesis: Chinese NLU needs its own benchmark because Chinese differs linguistically from English, and Chinese models will show headroom against human performance that English benchmarks no longer show.
contributions: A Chinese NLU benchmark covering a variety of sentence classification and machine reading comprehension tasks (9 tasks, 2 newly created).
A large-scale raw corpus (214 GB, ~76 billion words) for general-purpose Chinese pre-training.
A diagnostic evaluation dataset developed by linguists, including phenomena unique to Chinese.
A toolkit (PyCLUE) and an online leaderboard with an auto-evaluation system.

method.summary: Nine Chinese NLU tasks (3 single-sentence, 3 sentence-pair, 3 MRC) are collected or created and assigned one metric each. Nine pre-trained Chinese transformers are fine-tuned per task with an added output layer and scored against human performance. A 514-pair hand-written NLI diagnostic set probes nine linguistic phenomena, and a leaderboard with a 'certified' mark for reproducible open-source submissions is provided.
method.task: Chinese NLU benchmark: classification, sentence-pair, NLI, coreference, span-extraction and multiple-choice MRC

training.objective: supervised fine-tuning per task: pooled output to classifier (classification); two fully connected layers predicting start and end (span MRC); shared classifier scoring candidate-context pairs (multiple choice)
training.regularisation: early stopping to select best checkpoint
training.hardware: Cloud TPUs from Google TensorFlow Research Cloud acknowledged; no per-run hardware given
training.seeds: each model fine-tuned three times; the run with best dev performance is reported on test

other.hyperparameters: chosen on dev per model; summary said to be in Table 6 in the Appendix, which is not in this PDF
other.implementation: TensorFlow and PyTorch; toolkit PyCLUE in TensorFlow

inference.samples: 3 fine-tuning runs per model-task, best-dev run's test score reported

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction correct; used for all tasks except CMRC 2018

metrics.name: Avg
metrics.definition: average of all tasks (unweighted, inferred from table caption 'average of all tasks')

eval.protocol: Test-set scores from the best-dev of 3 fine-tuning runs. Human performance: OCNLI, CMRC 2018, ChID, C3 taken from their original papers; for TNEWS, AFQMC, CSL, IFLYTEK, CLUEWSC2020 three annotators label 100 randomly chosen test items after training on 30 to 50 dev items with discussion (SuperGLUE procedure), and the majority vote is scored. Diagnostic set: models fine-tuned on OCNLI and tested zero-shot on the 514 pairs. Leaderboard: submitted predictions scored automatically; scores marked 'certified' if the model is open source and the result reproduced.

evidence.quote: ask human annotators to label 100 randomly chosen items from the test set

results.claim: The best baseline (RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large) averages 74.90 across the nine tasks versus 85.09 for humans, about a 10-point gap.
results.setup: CLUE test sets, nine fine-tuned Chinese models, best-dev of 3 runs; human = majority vote on 100 test items for five tasks, published figures for four
results.table: Table 2, row RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large, column Avg; row Human, column Avg
results.note: Text says 'roughly 11 points lower than human performance on average' (Section 6.2) while conclusion says '~10%'; 85.09 - 74.90 = 10.19.

results.claim: Human performance is 98.0 on CLUEWSC2020 against 81.38 for the best model, a gap of about 17 points; the English WSC shows RoBERTa at 89% versus 100% for humans.
results.quote: the best score of models is far behind human performance
results.table: Table 3, row majority and row best model, column CLUEWSC2020

results.claim: On CSL, the best model (82.13) is above the mean annotator (80.0) and close to the majority vote (84.0); on AFQMC best model 76.5 vs majority 81.0.
results.setup: CSL test, best model vs three trained annotators
results.table: Table 3, row best model, column CSL; rows avg and majority
results.note: Table 3 'best model' for AFQMC is 76.5 while Table 2 gives RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large 76.55.

results.claim: TNEWS is the hardest task for both humans and machines: human majority 71.0 and best model 58.61.
results.quote: Surprisingly, the hardest dataset for both humans and machines is a single sentence task: TNEWS.
results.note: Authors' explanation: titles can fall under several categories while there is one gold label. Individual annotator scores range 57.0 to 73.0 (Table 3).

results.claim: ALBERT-tiny (about 1/20 of BERT-base parameters) loses almost 0 to roughly 12 points on single/pair tasks but drops up to 40 points on ChID.
results.quote: with a performance drop of up to 40 percentage compared with BERT-base (ChID)

results.claim: ALBERT-tiny gets 31.86 on C3, near chance for 2 to 4 options.
results.quote: ALBERT-tiny has a very low accuracy of about 32%

results.claim: XLNet-mid with a SentencePiece tokenizer does poorly on token-level span extraction (CMRC 2018 EM 66.51 vs 73.23 for BERT-wwm-ext-base).
results.quote: performs poorly in token level Chinese tasks like span-extraction

results.claim: On the diagnostic set (514 pairs, 9 phenomena), RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large scores 61.5 overall against 53.5 BERT-base and 54.7 XLNet-mid; the majority baseline is 35.1%.
results.setup: Models fine-tuned on OCNLI, tested on hand-written NLI diagnostic
results.quote: the highest accuracy is only about 61%
results.table: Table 4, row Total, columns BE 53.5, RO 61.5, XL 54.7

results.claim: Monotonicity is the hardest diagnostic category (43.3 for RoBERTa and XLNet, 41.7 for BERT); Time of event is easiest for RoBERTa (74.1).
results.setup: Monotonicity category of the diagnostic set (60 items)
results.quote: Monotonicity is the hardest, similar to GLUE diagnostics

results.claim: The lexical-semantics example (sad vs ugly, both starting with the character for hard) suggests models use a lexical-overlap heuristic.
results.setup: Diagnostic Table 4 lexical semantics example; two of three models predicted entailment where gold is neutral
results.note: Offered as a possible explanation citing McCoy et al. 2019, not tested.

results.claim: The pre-training corpus totals 214 GB, about 76 billion Chinese words, versus about 1.1 GB for Chinese Wikipedia.
results.quote: a total of 214 GB raw corpus with around 76 billion words are collected

results.claim: Results improve with larger models, more pre-training data, or whole word masking; RoBERTa-wwm-ext-large and ALBERT-xxlarge are best, especially on C3.
results.quote: 1) the model is larger, or 2) the model is trained with more pre-training data, or 3) whole word masking is used
results.note: The paper does not run controlled ablations of these three factors; the claim is read off the table of differently-built models.

limits: Human performance for five tasks rests on 100 randomly chosen test items and three annotators; individual annotators vary widely (TNEWS 57.0 to 73.0, IFLYTEK 50.0 to 80.0).
Test-set scores come from the best-dev of three fine-tuning runs with no variance reported, so small differences between models are not shown to be significant.
Baseline models differ at once in size, pre-training data and masking strategy, so the causes of gaps are not isolated.
Hyperparameters, filtering procedure and task examples live in an Appendix absent from this PDF.
The diagnostic set is small (514 pairs, 24 to 100 per category), and models are evaluated only after OCNLI fine-tuning.

No treatment of train/test contamination, leaderboard overfitting or private-test-set policy beyond the 'certified' mark; the pre-training corpus includes Common Crawl and Wikipedia without any overlap check against the task sets stated.
Authors concede the benchmark is open-ended and should be extended once models reach human level, possibly with performance as a function of model size (Li et al., 2020).
Dated: BERT-class encoders only; no generative LLMs.

terms.definition: we mark the score of a model as 'certified' if it is open-source, and we can reproduce the results
a small hand-crafted NLI set (entailment, contradiction, neutral) isolating linguistic phenomena, following GLUE

lineage.note: CLUE follows GLUE's multi-task benchmark and diagnostic design (Wang et al. 2018).
Human annotator training procedure and WSC-style task follow SuperGLUE (Wang et al. 2019).
Standard evaluation pipeline for sentence representations (Conneau and Kiela 2018).
Hu et al. 2020; chosen over XNLI because it is not translated.

lineage.work: Revisiting pre-trained models for Chinese NLP
lineage.note: Cui et al. 2020, source of wwm-ext models.
McCoy et al. 2019; lexical overlap heuristic invoked to explain diagnostic failure.
